Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
Counsel on record for the Appellant(s) : Suparna Srivastava for App. 1
Counsel on record for the Respondent(s) : Ashish Anand Bernard
Aditya Singh
Paramhans Sahni for Res.2
ORDER
IA NO. 1337 OF 2026
(For stay)
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON
1. The present Interlocutory Application has been filed by NHDC
Limited (“NHDC”/“Appellant”), in Appeal No 329 of 2026, seeking an
interim stay of the common order dated 30.03.2026 (“Impugned Order”)
passed by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (“CERC”/“
Central Commission”) in Petition Nos. 378/MP/2022 and 220/MP/2022,
whereby the Central Commission has allowed the claim of Respondent No.
2-M.P. Power Management Company Limited (“MPPMCL”) for
retrospective application of the corrigendum dated 29.03.2022 issued by
the Central Electricity Authority (“CEA”) in relation to the Techno-Economic
Clearance (“TEC”) for the Indira Sagar Project (“ISP”), implemented by the
Appellant, and has directed consequential revision of the Firm Power and
Design Energy of ISP as well as the Omkareshwar Project (“OSP”), along
with refund of the differential Secondary Energy Charges to Respondent
No. 2, the M.P. Power Management Company Limited ( “MPPMCL”).
Facts of the case
2. The Appellant, NHDC is engaged in the operation of the Indira
Sagar (ISP) and Omkareshwar (OSP) hydroelectric projects situated on the
river Narmada in Madhya Pradesh. The Design Energy, Firm Power and
Page 2 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
tariff for both projects had been determined by the Central Commission in
successive tariff orders on the basis of the respective Techno-Economic
Clearances (“TECs”) issued by the Central Electricity Authority (“CEA”) on
22.05.1984 for ISP and on 14.12.1993 for OSP.
3. On 29.03.2022, CEA issued a corrigendum to the TEC for ISP,
indicating the unit of water utilisation parameter ‘Q’ as Million Acre Feet
(“MAFt”) instead of Billion Cubic Meters (“BM³”). Thereafter, M.P. Power
Management Company Limited filed Petition Nos. 378/MP/2022 and
220/MP/2022 before the Central Commission seeking revision of the
Design Energy and Firm Power of the two projects (ISP & OSP) on the
basis of the said corrigendum.
4. By the Impugned Order dated 30.03.2026, the Central Commission
held that the earlier determination of Design Energy and Firm Power
required revision by considering ‘Q’ in MAFt and directed consequential
revision of the tariff for the relevant periods. The Central Commission
further directed the parties to reconcile the differential refund amount within
three months and directed the Appellant to refund the amount so
determined in 12 equal, interest-free instalments.
5. Aggrieved by the aforesaid directions, the Appellant has preferred
the accompanying Appeal 329 of 2026 under Section 111 of the Electricity
Act, 2003, challenging, inter alia, the retrospective application of the CEA
corrigendum and the reopening of tariff orders which, had already attained
finality. The Appellant contends that implementation of the Impugned Order
would entail substantial financial and regulatory consequences, including
retrospective reconciliation of accounts and disturbance of settled financial
and commercial arrangements.
Page 3 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
Analysis and Discussion
6. We have heard Mrs. Suparna Srivastava, the learned counsel
appearing on behalf of the Appellant- NHDC Limited, Mr. Aashish Anand
Bernard, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of Respondent No. 2-
MPPMCL, and have perused the written submissions filed by the parties,
the pleadings and other documents placed on record. The rival
submissions advanced by the parties are summarized hereunder:
Submissions urged on behalf of Appellant
7. The Appellant is a joint venture between NHPC Limited (51%) and
the Government of Madhya Pradesh (49%) and has implemented the 1000
MW Indira Sagar Project (“ISP”), which achieved COD on 25.08.2005, and
the 520 MW Omkareshwar Project (“OSP”), which achieved COD on
15.11.2007, in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The entire power generated
from these projects is purchased by Respondent No. 2 at the tariffs
determined by the Central Commission. The Appellant submits that the
‘ISP’ was implemented in accordance with TEC issued by CEA on
22.05.1984, which specified water utilisation in BM³, whereas the TEC for
‘OSP’ dated 14.12.1993 specified the corresponding water utilisation in
MAFt. Since ‘ISP’ functions as the mother reservoir supplying water to the
downstream ‘OSP’ for power generation, use of two different units of
measurement for the interconnected projects would result in an anomaly in
the computation of water availability, Design Energy and Firm Power and
in the tariff filings for both projects BM³, has been considered as the unit for
water utilization. The Central Commission determined tariffs accordingly
over successive tariff periods, and Respondent No. 2, having participated
in the tariff proceedings and has accepted the tariff determinations without
Page 4 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
challenging the use of BM³ for ‘ISP’ & ‘OSP’ and such tariff orders have
attained finality.
8. It is submitted that, in Petition No. 106/GT/2020, filed for
determination of tariff for the period 2019–24, Respondent No. 2 had raised
the discrepancy in the unit of water utilisation and sought revision of the
TEC and the corresponding tariff determinations for past periods. However,
Central Commission vide Order dated 06.01.2022, declined to undertake
such revision at that stage, observing that Firm Power and energy
generation were to be reviewed on the basis of actual data upon completion
of the three stages of water utilisation. The Appellant contends that
Respondent No. 2, having accepted the said finding, is precluded from
raising the same claim afresh, which is barred by the principles of res
judicata, as recognised in “State of U.P. v. Nawab Hussain, (1977) 2 SCC
806”, and “Union of India v. N. Murugesan, (2022) 2 SCC 25”.
9. CEA, after more than four decades from the issuance of the original
TEC for ‘ISP’, issued a Corrigendum dated 29.03.2022, stating that “BM³
(Billion Cubic Metre) may be read as ‘MAF’ (Million Acre Feet)”, without
specifying any retrospective application. Relying upon the principle that a
substantive amendment cannot ordinarily operate retrospectively in the
absence of express authority, particularly where vested rights and
concluded transactions are affected, as discussed in “Bharat Sanchar
Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd.”, (2022) 20 SCC 96, the
Appellant contends that the Corrigendum could operate only prospectively.
10. Central Commission, vide the Impugned Order, has allowed the
petitions filed by Respondent No. 2, holding that the unit of water utilisation
ought to have been considered as MAFt instead of BM³ and that the
Page 5 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
Corrigendum dated 29.03.2022 relates back to the original TEC and
consequently, held that the Firm Power, Design Energy and corresponding
tariff for the relevant past periods were erroneously determined and warrant
review based on equitable consideration, and that the excess Secondary
Energy Charges allegedly paid by Respondent No. 2 were liable to be
refunded. The Central Commission has further held that the petitions were
within limitation, as the right to sue accrued upon issuance of the
Corrigendum, and that the proceedings did not constitute forum shopping
or abuse of process. Central Commission directed revision of Firm Power,
Design Energy and the consequential tariff computations for FY 2010–11
to FY 2018–19, and directed the parties to reconcile the amounts payable,
with the Appellant being required to refund the differential amount in 12
equal, interest-free instalments. The amounts reconciled pursuant to the
Impugned Order are Rs109.58 Crore for ‘ISP’ and Rs 46.55 Crore for
‘OSP’, aggregating to Rs156.13 Crore, payable in 12 instalments of
approximately Rs13.01 Crore each.
11. The Appellant submits that the Impugned Order suffers from various
infirmities like the CEA Corrigendum dated 29.03.2022 is silent on
retrospective applicability, and its application to past tariff periods alters the
technical basis of tariff determination and imposes substantial financial
liabilities; therefore, the same cannot be treated as a mere clerical
correction, as held in Vijay v. UOI & Ors.*, (2023) 17 SCC 455; Sree
Sankaracharya University of Sanskrit v. Dr. Manu & Anr., (2023) 19
SCC 30; Bharat Vijay Mills v. UOI, 2018 SCC OnLine Guj 373. It is further
contended that Respondent No. 2 seeks to reopen concluded Tariff Orders
on the basis of the Corrigendum, although the alleged discrepancy in the
unit of water utilisation was discernible from the inception and could have
been raised in the original proceedings. The Corrigendum cannot constitute
Page 6 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
“new and important matter or evidence” within the meaning of Order XLVII
Rule 1 CPC, and the Central Commission, while exercising review
jurisdiction, has failed to apply the settled principles governing such
jurisdiction. In support, reliance is placed upon Kamlesh Verma v.
Mayawati, (2013) 8 SCC 320; U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. v. NTPC Ltd.,
(2009) 6 SCC 235. The Regulation 103 of the CERC (Conduct of Business)
Regulations, 1999 prescribes a limitation period of 45 days for review and
that the finding that the cause of action arose only upon issuance of the
Corrigendum is erroneous, as the alleged discrepancy existed from the
inception. It is also contended that the Central Commission could not grant
unpleaded or unprayed monetary relief on equitable grounds, as equity
cannot override settled law, as held in Raghunath Rai Bareja v. Punjab
National Bank, (2007) 2 SCC 230. The Appellant further submits that the
issue concerning the unit of water utilisation is barred by the principles of
res judicata, having already been considered in the earlier proceedings,
and that the Central Commission has re-adjudicated the issue without
addressing the Appellant’s objection on this ground. It is also contended
that Respondent No. 2 sought only declaratory relief in Petition Nos.
378/MP/2022 and 220/MP/2022 and did not seek any consequential relief,
and that grant of such relief in the absence of a specific prayer is
impermissible under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, particularly
where further relief was available but not sought, as held in Muni Lal v.
Oriental Fire & General Insurance Co. Ltd., (1996) 1 SCC 90; Ranbir
Singh v. Executive Engineer, (2011) 15 SCC 453. The retrospective
revision of Design Energy, Firm Power and consequential tariff for
concluded periods would unsettle established financial and regulatory
arrangements and is contrary to Section 62(4) of the Electricity Act, 2003,
as cited in BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. DERC, (2023) 4 SCC 788; Delhi
Jal Board v. DERC & Ors., Order dated 04.01.2013 in Appeal No. 157
Page 7 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
of 2012;PTC India Ltd. v. CERC, (2010) 4 SCC 603; Shree Siddhbali
Steels Ltd. v. State of U.P., (2011) 3 SCC 193, . Furthermore,
Respondent No. 2 is pursuing substantially overlapping reliefs before the
Madhya Pradesh High Court and the Central Commission, which amounts
to forum shopping and is impermissible in law, as cited in Union of India
& Ors. v. Cipla Ltd. & Anr., (2017) 5 SCC 262.
12. CERC has failed to appreciate the cascading financial and
regulatory consequences of the impugned directions, particularly when the
corresponding power purchase costs have already been accounted for and
passed through in ARR and retail tariffs applicable to end consumers. The
Appellant submits that the balance of convenience lies in preserving the
existing position pending adjudication of the Appeal, as failure to grant
interim protection would cause irreparable injury to the Appellant.
Appellant, therefore, satisfies the three essential requirements for grant of
interim stay, namely, the existence of a prima facie case, balance of
convenience in its favour, and the likelihood of irreparable injury, as
recognised by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad
Singh, (1992) 1 SCC 719, and Colgate Palmolive (India) Ltd. v.
Hindustan Lever Ltd., (1999) 7 SCC 1.
Submissions Urged on behalf of Respondent No.2
13. It is submitted that Corrigendum dated 29.03.2022 issued by the
CEA has never been challenged by the Appellant before any court of law
and, therefore, NHDC cannot now dispute its applicability by questioning
its date of operation. The Corrigendum relates back to the original order
and applies retrospectively, unlike an amendment, which operates from the
date of its issuance and therefore consequences flowing from the
Page 8 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
Corrigendum must ensure to the benefit of Respondent No. 2, Further it is
clear that “Corrigendum” is not an “Amendment” and only an “Amendment”
is applicable from the date of issuance. It is further contended that the
Appellant was consulted by the CEA before issuance of the Corrigendum.
The CERC has conclusively dealt with this issue in paragraphs 28–31 of
the Impugned Order. It is also submitted that the “Corrigendum” relates
back to its original order and a perusal of corrigendum dated 29.03.2022,
clearly shows that the corrigendum has been issued to the letter of the year
1989 wherein the CEA has stated that the BMQ may be read as MAFt. In
support of the aforesaid submissions, reliance is placed upon Polyplex
Corporation Ltd. v. Union of India & Others, 2014 SCC OnLine All
5211.
14. The Respondent No. 2 submits that no review of the previous Tariff
Orders has been sought by it or undertaken by CERC, as the formula for
calculation of Design Energy had been provided by NHDC itself, and only
the values to be incorporated into the said formula required reconsideration
in view of the corrigendum dated 29.03.2022 issued by the CEA to its letter,
whereby the unit of water utilisation for irrigation, i.e., ‘Q’, was corrected
from BM³ to MAFt. Accordingly, the Design Energy was required to be
recalculated by considering the value of ‘Q’ in MAFt in all Tariff Orders
issued by this Commission since 2010 in respect of the Indira Sagar Power
Station. The CERC has rightly observed in Paragraph 25 that “The
Petitioner had paid excess secondary charges to the Appellant on account
of the incorrect consideration of the unit water utilization for irrigation ‘Q’ as
BM3 instead of MAfT by CEA in its TEC in respect of ISHEP and the
Commission in its Tariff Orders. Further, in Paragraphs 40–42, the CERC
has clearly held that there is no change in the approved Annual Fixed
Charges (AFC), Capacity Charges or Energy Charges, and that any
Page 9 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
revision is confined only to Secondary Energy Charges, which constitute
an incentive payment to the Generator over and above the AFC. The
objection regarding limitation is also not sustainable, as the cause of action
accrued in favour of Respondent No. 2 on 29.03.2022, upon issuance of
the corrigendum, whereas the Petition was filed in August 2022. Further, a
correction or corrigendum precedes an inherent admission on the part of
the person making correction/issuing corrigendum that the initial document
or initial authored material has some mistake and admitting this mistake
the same is being rectified/corrected and hence a correction/corrigendum,
in support of which reliance is placed upon “State of Rajasthan and
Another v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. and Another, (2004) 7 SCC 673”.
15. Appellant, vide letter dated 02.11.2022, had approached the CEA
seeking clarification regarding the applicability and effective date of
implementation of the corrigendum dated 29.03.2022, and it is the
Appellant’s own case that the corrigendum should be applicable from the
date of its issuance. However, CEA did not respond to the said letter, nor
did the Appellant challenge the corrigendum. Thus, the conduct of the
Appellant demonstrates its acceptance of the corrigendum, and the
Appellant cannot now raise objections to deny Respondent No. 2 the
benefits accruing therefrom. Further, the principle of res judicata is not
applicable in the present case, as the CERC, in its order dated 06.01.2022,
particularly in Para 68, observed that there was no reason to revise the
Design Energy (DE) “at this stage”, as also evident from Paragraphs 66–
67 of the said order. Therefore, upon issuance of the corrigendum dated
29.03.2022, the requisite circumstances had arisen for Respondent No. 2
to file the Petition seeking revision of the Design Energy, which has been
allowed by the CERC, and consequently, the bar of res judicata does not
apply.
Page 10 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
16. Further, CERC has rightly held in Paragraph 41 of the Impugned
Order that there is no change in the total actual energy generated during
the disputed period and that the effect is limited only to the reclassification
of energy from Secondary Energy to SDE/DE. The illustration provided by
the CERC in the said paragraph further clearly demonstrates that the total
generation remains unchanged and that only the Secondary Energy is
affected by the change in the unit of water utilisation from BM³ to MAFt.
The change in the unit of consumptive water utilisation, i.e., ‘Q’, from BCM
to MAF in the formula determined by the CERC for both ISP and OSP
power stations of the Appellant does not materially affect the recovery of
fixed charges allowed by the CERC under various orders for the period
from 2010–11 to 2018–19.
17. It is contended that, as per TEC, the permissible Design Energy for
ISPS for the period from 2010–11 to 2018–19 (i.e., the First Stage) is 1,980
MUs. However, the Appellant has been computing and claiming Design
Energy on the basis of a formula considering the value of ‘Q’ in BM³,
resulting in Design Energy varying from 1,900.93 MUs to 1,423.28 MUs,
whereas, upon considering the value of ‘Q’ in MAFt, the corresponding
Design Energy varies from 1,958.91 MUs to 1,655.89 MUs. Similarly, for
OSPS, the Design Energy specified in the TEC is 1,166.57 MUs, whereas
the Appellant has been computing and claiming Design Energy by
considering the value of ‘Q’ in BM³, resulting in Design Energy varying from
865.05 MUs to 736.45 MUs, while consideration of ‘Q’ in MAFt results in
the corresponding Design Energy varying from 896.44 MUs to 848.77 MUs.
Thus, the aforesaid figures indicate that, in both projects, the Appellant has
been claiming Design Energy substantially lower than that specified in the
TEC, as a consequence of which the energy generated over and above the
Page 11 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
lower Design Energy so computed is treated as Secondary Energy, thereby
resulting in a higher quantum of Secondary Energy and, in turn, a higher
incentive claim.
OUR CONSIDERATION
18. It is an admitted position that Techno Economic clearance for the
ISP (1000 MW) was granted vide letter dated 22.05.1984 and that for OSP
(520 MW) project was granted vide letter dated 14.12.1993, and ISP
project achieved COD on 25.08.2005, and the OSP, achieved COD on
15.11.2007, and has been supplying power to Respondent No 2. The
Corrigendum to TEC of ISP has been issued on 29.03.2022, clarifying that
unit of water utilization (Q) indicated in the TEC of ISP as BM3 to be
considered as MAFt. Thereafter, Respondent No 2 filed petitions before the
Central Commission, seeking revision of Firm Power and Design Energy
for ISP and OSP based on the corrigendum to TEC issued by CEA, revising
unit of water utilization from BM3 to MAFt, which led to revision of energy
for these projects for the tariff period from 2010-11 to 2019-24 in the
Impugned Order and it was held that “Computation of Firm Power, Design
Energy and the corresponding energy beyond the design energy have
been revised on the value of Q MFBt for the period 2010-11 to 2018-19”.
Accordingly, the design energy of both ISP and OSP was revised.
19. Appellant and Respondent No 2 were directed to reconcile the
amount, and such an amount to be refunded by Appellant in twelve interest
-free installments to MPPMCL. The said amount has been reconciled and
has been quantified at Rs109.58 Crore for ISP and Rs 46.55 Crore for OSP,
aggregating to Rs156.13 Crore (up to FY 2018-19), payable in 12
instalments of approximately Rs13.01 Crore each in terms of Impugned
Page 12 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
Order. It is further stated in the Impugned Order, that design Energy for
the year FY 2019-20 onwards shall be considered in the truing – up
petitions for the year 2019-24, filed by NHDC, which are already under
consideration before the Central Commission. Admittedly, the Appellant
has not challenged the Corrigendum letter to TEC dated 29.03.2022 and
stated to be already made applicable prospectively. Appellant is only
aggrieved by the retrospective application of the Corrigendum, leading to
re-computation of design Energy and Firm Power for the period FY 2010-
11 onwards and accordingly, seeks stay of the Impugned Order pending
disposal of the Appeal.
20. The grant or refusal of interlocutory relief is covered by three well
established principles viz., (1) whether the Appellant has made out a prima
facie case, (2) whether the balance of convenience is in their favour i.e.,
whether it would cause greater inconvenience to them if interim relief is not
granted than the inconvenience which the opposite party would be put to if
it is granted, and (3) whether the Appellant would suffer irreparable injury.
With the first condition as a sine quo non, at least two conditions should be
satisfied by the Appellant conjunctively, and a mere proof of fulfilment of
one of the three conditions does not entitle them to the grant of interlocutory
relief in their favour. (Nawab Mir Barkat Ali Khan v. Nawab Zulfiquar Jah
Bahadur, AIR 1975 AP 187; Gone Rajamma v. Chennamaneni Mohan
Rao, (2010) 3 ALD 175; Kishoresinh Ratansinh Jadeja v. Maruti Corpn,
(2009) 11 SCC 229; Best Sellers Retail (India) Private Ltd. v. Aditya
Birla Nuvo Ltd., (2012) 6 SCC 792; State of Mizoram v. Pooja Fortune
Private Limited, 2019 SCC OnLine SC 1741).
21. In the present case, it has been mainly contended by Respondent-
MPPMCL that the letter dated 29.03.2022 is in the form of corrigendum to
Page 13 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
the TEC issued for ISP on 22.05.1984 and therefore there is no bar in its
retrospective application. The distinction between a corrigendum and an
addendum is doctrinally clear. A corrigendum, derived from the Latin
corrigere, is issued to rectify an error, omission, or misstatement in the
original instrument; its function is corrective, and it operates to heal a defect
in the text already promulgated. An addendum, by contrast, stems from the
Latin addere, and is employed to supplement the original instrument with
additional matter; its function is enlarging, and it operates to extend or
clarify the scope of what has been set forth. Therefore, while a
corrigendum cures, an addendum augments. The two are not
interchangeable. The issuance of a corrigendum is legally permissible
only to rectify clerical or typographical errors, or to correct accidental slips
or omissions, so that the record reflects the true intention of the authority
at the time of the original order. The issue in the present case is whether
the letter dated 29.03.2022 can be considered a corrigendum or to be
considered an addendum and even if at this stage it is assumed to be in
the form of corrigendum, can it alter the concluded tariff determination since
FY 2010-2011.
22. The doctrine of functus officio and the principle of finality of orders
restrain a regulatory authority from altering its concluded tariff orders when
such an order has been acted upon and rights have crystallized. We also
take note that corrigendum letter dated 29.03.2022 have been issued in the
case of TEC for ISP as water utilisation(Q) unit has been mentioned in
both MAFt (Million Acre Feet) and BM³ (Billion Cubic Metres), however in
the original TEC for ‘OSP project, the water utilisation (Q) has been
mentioned only in MAFt, however energy calculations have been done
considering water utilisation in BM3, same as that of ISP and Respondent
No.2 - MPPMCL has accepted such a determination since its
Page 14 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
commissioning. The tariff orders are quasi-judicial determinations passed
under statutory mandate. Once such orders have been subjected to
true-up, appellate scrutiny, or have otherwise attained finality, they merge
into the regulatory continuum.
23. The corrigendum letter dated 29.03.2022 purports to change the
unit of water utilisation in a Techno-Economic Clearance (TEC) issued four
decades earlier for ISP, substituting BM³ with MAFt. Such a change,
though ostensibly clerical, has substantive consequences because it alters
the design energy computation, which in turn impacts tariff determination.
Once tariff orders have been passed, subjected to appellate scrutiny, and
implemented over the years, they cannot, prima facie, be reopened
retrospectively on the even on the strength of a corrigendum.
24. It is also pertinent to note that Respondent-MPPMCL had disputed
the unit of water utilisation considered in the tariff petition for determination
of tariff for the year 2014-19 and MPPMCL vide letter dated 17.05.2021,
and MPPMCL, approached the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) seeking
a review of the TEC for ISP, which subsequently resulted in the issue of
corrigendum letter dated 29.03.2022 . The Central Commission in its order
dated 06.01.2022, passed in the proceedings to truing up of Annual Fixed
Charges for the tariff period 2014-19 and for determination of tariff for the
tariff period 2019-24, observed that the ongoing development stage would
cease in 2024 as per Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal ( “NWDT”) Award
and as the firm Power/energy and secondary energy generation will also
be subjected to review based on actual available data. Accordingly, the
Central Commission held that MPPMCL’s prayer for the revision of TEC of
the project was not warranted at that stage, and no revision of design
energy was undertaken.
Page 15 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
25. However, under the Impugned Order, design energy for both ISP &
OSP has been re-determined with retrospective effect from FY 2010-2011
onwards, that is, prior to conclusion of ongoing development stage. While
the rival submissions of the parties would require detailed examination at
the stage of final hearing, we are prima facie of the view that permitting
such retrospective alteration, at the interim stage, would have the effect of
unsettling vested rights, and undermine regulatory certainty.
26. As noticed hereinabove, both MPPMCL and the Appellant have
acted for several years on the basis of the TEC then in force, and the
determination and settlement of design energy and secondary energy have
been carried out accordingly. Any retrospective revision of such
foundational parameters would have significant regulatory and financial
consequences. In these circumstances, and having regard to the
observations recorded above, we are satisfied that the balance of
convenience lies in favour of the Appellant. It is also noted that the
Appellant has stated that it has commenced computation of design energy
in accordance with the corrigendum prospectively.
27. For the reasons delineated above, we are satisfied that the
Appellant has made out a prima facie case for grant of interim protection
and that the balance of convenience also lies in its favour. Accordingly,
operation of the Impugned Order dated 30.03.2026 passed by the Central
Commission, insofar as it directs payment of reconciled amount, is hereby
stayed, pending adjudication of the appeal on merits. We also make it clear
that the present order shall not affect any payment already made by the
Appellant to MPPMCL in compliance with the Impugned Order, and status
quo in respect thereof shall be maintained.
Page 16 of 17

Order in IA No. 1337 of 2026 in Appeal No. 329 of 2026
Needless to state that this interim arrangement is provisional and
shall be subject to the final determination of the issues arising in the
appeal. All observations made in this order are prima facie and shall not
prejudice the rights and contentions of either party at the stage of final
hearing. The Interlocutory application is disposed of accordingly.
APPEAL NO. 329 OF 2026
Respondents are granted six weeks to file Reply to the Appeal and
Appellant to file rejoinder, if any, within four weeks thereafter. Registry to
verify and after completion of pleadings and, thereafter, the Appeal to be
included in the ‘List of Finals’ to be taken up from there in their turn.
PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT ON THIS 02nd DAY OF
NOVEMBER, 2026.

ORDER
IA NO. 862 OF 2026
(interim relief)
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON
1. The present Interlocutory Application has been filed in Appeal No
194 of 2026, under Section 111 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (“Act”) by
NHPC Limited (“Appellant”/ “NHPC”) assailing the Order dated
16.03.2026 (“Impugned Order”) passed by the Andhra Pradesh
Electricity Regulatory Commission (“State Commission”/ “APERC”) in
O.P. No. 65 of 2025, with respect to the limited issue that the State
Commission has disallowed and altered the trading margin of 7 paise/kWh
payable to the Appellant under the Battery Energy Storage System
(“BESS”) framework or margin of 0.5% of Capacity Charges. The
Impugned Order otherwise approves the Battery Energy Storage Sale
Agreements (“BESSA”) dated 10.07.2025, the associated Battery Energy
Storage Purchase Agreements (“BESPA”) dated 16.07.2025, for
procurement of 500 MW/1000 MWh BESS capacity and adoption of the
discovered tariffs for a period of 12 years.
2. In the Impugned Order, State Commission while purporting to adopt
the tariff of Battery Energy Storage System ( BESS) under Section 63,
substituted the margin of 7 paise/kWh as agreed with 0.5% of Capacity
Charges relying on the Clause 2.G(4) of the MoP Guidelines dated
10.03.2022 which permits an Intermediary Procurer to charge a trading
margin of “7 paise/kWh OR 0.5% of Capacity Charges (whichever
applies)”
Page 3 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
3. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order, the Appellant preferred the
Appeal and in the present Application seeking following interim reliefs: -
a. Stay the operation and effect of the Impugned Order dated
16.03.2026 passed by the Ld. APERC in O.P. No. 65 of 2025, to
the extent it disallows and substitutes the trading margin of 7
paise/kWh and directs modification of the executed contractual
framework;
b. Direct the Respondents to maintain status quo with respect to the
contractual arrangements under the BESSA dated 10.07.2025
and BESPA dated 16.07.2025, including the trading margin of 7
paise/kWh payable to the Appellant;
c. Pass any such order that this Hon’ble Tribunal may deem fit in
the interest of justice.
DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS
4. We have heard Mr. S. Venkatesh Learned Counsel appearing on
behalf of the Appellant/Applicant, and Mr. Rudrajit Ghosh, learned counsel
for the Respondent Nos. 2 to 4 and perused the written submissions filed
by parties, which are summarized hereunder, and other documents on
record:
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF APPELLANT
5. It is submitted that once the Commission approved the project
explicitly stating the trading margin of 7 paise/unit, a tariff is discovered
through a bidding process and the parties are entitled to execute the
contract on settled terms and the same cannot be subsequently altered
by defeating the legitimate expectation created by its own representation.
State Commission’s own letter dated 04.07.2025 (“Tariff, Trading Margin,
and BESSA”) which was issued subsequent to examination of
submissions, relevant documents and formats of agreements, without
qualification or reservation, recorded a trading margin of Rs.0.07/unit
payable to the Appellant, pursuant to which the BESSA dated 10.07.2025
Page 4 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
and the BESPAs dated 16.07.2025 and 28.07.2025 were executed fixing
the margin at 7 paise/kWh under Article 1.1. It is further submitted that the
Impugned Order records no intervening finding of illegality, non-
compliance or new fact to justify departure from agreed contractual
framework. It is merely a change of opinion on two dates by different
reading of Clause 2.G(4), and same is impermissible without cogent
reasons ( “Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed
Industries”; (1993) 1 SCC 71, “Navjyoti Coop. Group Housing
Society v. Union of India”; (1992) 4 SCC 477, “ State of Jharkhand v.
Brahmaputra Metallics Ltd.”; 2020 SCC OnLine SC 968).
6. Respondents, in their reply has placed reliance on Article 1.1 to
contend that the transaction concerns a sale of “capacity”, however
Respondents themselves executed the BESSA without demur, sought
only its approval and not its amendment in O.P. No. 65 of 2025, and raised
no objection to the 7 paise/kWh margin at the RfS stage, at execution, or
at the public hearing dated 05.02.2026, and therefore, cannot now be
permitted to approbate and reprobate as held in Rajasthan State
Industrial Development & Investment Corporation v. Diamond & Gem
Development Corporation Ltd., (2013) 5 SCC 470; R.N. Gosain v.
Yashpal Dhir, (1992) 4 SCC 683; Premlata v. Naseeb Bee, (2022) 6
SCC 585.
7. It is contended that the Clause 2.G(4) of the BESS Guidelines
recognises both the 7 paise/kWh and 0.5% of Capacity Charges
formulations “as applicable”, without confining either to a particular class
of procurement, energy transaction for the former and capacity transaction
for the latter or using the expression “respectively”, thereby leaves no
room for the Commission to select one formulation in substitution of that
Page 5 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
stipulated in the procurement documents. Guidelines contemplate
competitive procurement in terms of BESS capacity while nevertheless
retaining both formulations under Clause 2.5G(4). The parties have been
given liberty to have contract on mutual consent on trading margin as per
the Regulation 8(1)(d) of Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of trading license and other
related matters) Regulations, 2020, which stipulates that for transactions
under long term contracts, the trading margin shall be decided mutually
between the Trading Licensee and the seller and accordingly, both parties
have mutually signed the contract on Trading Margin @ 07 Paise/unit be
kept exclusive of tariff.
8. Appellant does not seek the recharacterization of the procurement
as energy-based, but submits that a capacity-based bidding parameter,
does not textually or conceptually, render the 7 paise/kWh limb of Clause
2.G(4) inapplicable and that, had the Guidelines intended the 0.5% metric
to mandatorily apply wherever the tariff is expressed through Capacity
Charges, same would have been stipulated in Clause 2.G(4).
9. Further RfS itself requires buying entity to off-take both contracted
capacity and energy, and prescribes scheduled charging and discharge
in MWh, and requires daily charge-discharge cycles, measures availability
with reference to actual and scheduled energy injection/drawal, and
accordingly the executed BESSA itself combines the sale of BESS
Capacity with a Trading Margin denominated in paise/kWh.
10. It is submitted that Section 63 confines the Respondent
Commission to adoption, not determination, of a tariff discovered through
transparent bidding. Trading Margin at 7 paise /kWh is not itself a
Page 6 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
competitive discovered bid parameter but the Commission cannot
substitute its own preferred Trading Margin unless agreed formulation
itself is prohibited by the Guidelines. The reliance has been placed on
Energy Watchdog v. CERC, (2017) 14 SCC 80 to support the contention
that Commission’s statutory function is just to adopt the tariff; SECI v.
DERC, SECI v. UPERC and Ayana Ananthapuramu Solar v. APERC
wherein mutually agreed Trading Margins in long-term transactions has
been protected.
11. Finding in the Impugned Order that Appellant bears zero risk is
contrary to the express terms of the BESPA, Article 14.4.1 whereof, by a
non-obstante clause, provides that the Appellant's payment obligation to
the BESS Developer shall not be on a back-to-back basis, and Article
10.4.7 whereof places the cost of the Appellant's Letter of Credit upon the
Appellant itself.
12. The Appellant submits that Paragraph 26 of the Impugned Order
goes beyond adoption and directs “the DISCOMs shall amend the
BESSAs” amendment of a contractual term the Appellant never agreed
to, contrary to GUVNL v. Solar Semiconductor Power Co. (India) Pvt.
Ltd., (2017) 16 SCC 498, wherein it is held that even where a regulator
may possess tariff jurisdiction, it cannot compel a party to enter into a
contract on the basis of a redetermined tariff or vary the terms of the
concluded contract by invoking regulatory jurisdiction. Therefore, the
direction to rewrite Article 1.1 therefore raises a substantial prima facie
issue independent of the ultimate quantum of Trading Margin.
13. Further, the Paragraph 28 of the Impugned order makes approval
of the BESSA/BESPAs contingent upon compliance with amendment
Page 7 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
stated in Paragraph 26, while Articles 2.1.3 and 2.1.4 of the BESPA tie
Tariff Adoption within stipulated time and Financial Closure and the
Scheduled Commissioning Date to the tariff-adoption order, respectfully.
Therefore, the Appellant is not in the position of either altering a concluded
contractual term which is the very subject matter of the Appeal or exposing
implementation of the projects to contractual consequences flowing from
delayed/conditional adoption.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF RESPONDENT NO. 2 to 4
14. It is submitted that the interim relief sought, being in substance a
prayer to set aside the very direction under challenge in the Appeal,
amounts to grant of final relief at the interim stage and ought not to be
granted, relying on Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine v.
Dr. Salma Khatoon, (2021) 20 SCC 61 and Super Cassettes Industries
Ltd. v. Music Broadcast Pvt. Ltd., (2012) 5 SCC 488;; and that there is,
in any event, no pre-existing ‘status quo’ capable of restoration, since the
BESS facility is yet to be commissioned and the Impugned Order was
passed at the stage of preliminary approval of the BESSA and BESPA, so
that the prayer for 'status quo' mischaracterizes what is, in substance, a
prayer for final relief;
15. Appellant has failed to make a prima facie case for interim relief.
That the BESSA and BESPA are, on their own terms, agreements for
purchase and sale of BESS Capacity as borne out by the Preamble and
specific provisions concerning under “purchase and sale of contracted
capacity” and Article V of the BESSA record that the Answering
Respondents agreed to purchase, and the Appellant agreed to sell, the
500 MW/1000 MWh of 'BESS Capacity' procured by the Appellant from
Page 8 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
the BESSDs under back-to-back BESPAs. Further, Article 1.1 which
states that the 7 paise/kWh margin is 'for sale of BESS capacity', and by
Clauses 3.1 and 3.2 of the RfS (referring to 'total capacity' and 'Contracted
Capacity' respectfully), a characterization of the BESSA being for sale and
purchase of capacity has been admitted by the Appellant, at paragraphs
10-11 of its Rejoinder in the present Application and paragraph 19 of its
Rejoinder in the Appeal, to be 'not disputed'.
16. It is submitted that Section 63 requires the Respondent Commission
to examine whether a tariff has been discovered through a transparent
bidding process in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central
Government, so that non-compliance with the BESS Guidelines can found
interference even in the proceedings under Section 63 of the Act, relying
on JSW Renew Energy v. CERC, 2025 SCC OnLine APTEL 56.
17. Clause 2.G(4), prescribes trading margin of two types, i.e., “7
paise/kWh” or “0.5% of Capacity Charges” depending on the BESSA and
BESPA being for purchase and sale of either “energy” or “capacity”
respectively. Further, as per BESS Guidelines 2022, trading margin
'applicable' for the purchase and sale of contracted capacity, as against
units of energy, is “0.5% of the Capacity Charges”. The Respondents also
dispute the Appellant's reliance on Ayana Ananthapuramu Solar v.
APERC and SECI v. UPERC, since the guidelines considered in those
cases left the margin to mutual consent, unlike Clause 2.G(4), which
admits no such negotiation; and that the direction to amend the BESSA is
consistent with Article 4.7 thereof, which itself provides for amendment to
ensure compliance with applicable law.
Page 9 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
18. It is submitted that the Commission has exercised its jurisdiction
vested u/s 63 of the Electricity Act and with the applicable Guidelines in
terms of the BESSA, specifically Article 4.7 which provides for
amendments to be made to the BESSA to bring the same in compliance
with applicable laws. Therefore, the Appellant's obligations as
Intermediary Procurer afford no ground for interim relief, since the
Impugned Order itself records and accounts for such obligations in
prescribing the applicable margin, and the adequacy of a Guideline-
mandated margin cannot be reopened at the interim stage.
Our consideration
19. The Issue in consideration pertains to substituting the Trading
margin of 7 paisa/ unit as agreed in the BESSA between the Appellant
and Respondent –Discom by .5 % of capacity charges under the
Impugned Order , while approving the Battery Energy Storage Sale
Agreements (“BESSA”) dated 10.07.2025, and associated Battery Energy
Storage Purchase Agreements (“BESPA”) dated 16.07.2025, for
procurement of Battery Energy storage System, via Appellant, the
Intermediary Procurer. Vide the present application, Appellant is seeking
stay of the Impugned Order.
20 The grant or refusal of interlocutory relief is covered by three well
established principles viz., (1) whether the Appellant has made out a
prima facie case, (2) whether the balance of convenience is in their favour
i.e., whether it would cause greater inconvenience to them if interim relief
is not granted than the inconvenience which the opposite party would be
put to if it is granted, and (3) whether the Appellant would suffer irreparable
injury. With the first condition as a sine quo non, at least two conditions
Page 10 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
should be satisfied by the Appellant conjunctively, and a mere proof of
fulfilment of one of the three conditions does not entitle them to the grant
of interlocutory relief in their favour. (Nawab Mir Barkat Ali Khan v. Nawab
Zulfiquar Jah Bahadur, AIR 1975 AP 187; Gone Rajamma v.
Chennamaneni Mohan Rao, (2010) 3 ALD 175; Kishoresinh Ratansinh
Jadeja v. Maruti Corpn, (2009) 11 SCC 229; Best Sellers Retail (India)
Private Ltd. v. Aditya Birla Nuvo Ltd., (2012) 6 SCC 792; State of Mizoram
v. Pooja Fortune Private Limited, 2019 SCC OnLine SC 1741).
21. In the present case, State Commission granted in-principle approval
on 09.04.2025 for procurement of 500 MW/1000 MWh Battery Storage
Project at three locations and appointment of NHPC-the Appellant as
Implementing Agency. NHPC proceeded ahead with the competitive
bidding process and discovered the tariff for three identified project
locations. The Respondent, vide its letter dated 26.06.2025 informed the
State Commission with regard to completion of bidding process and
sought approval for discovered tariff and it also informed that as per RfS
provision, the Discom were required to pay a trading margin of 7 paisa per
unit to NHPC- the Appellant State Commission. State Commission taking
note of the submissions, vide letter dated 04.07.2025, conveyed that “
Commission is inclined to permit APDISCOMs to initiate further steps for
the procurement of BSES services as stated above, following its in-
principle approval’. Accordingly the BESSA dated 10.07.2025, between
Appellant and APDISCOMs and associated Battery Energy Storage
Purchase Agreements between Appellant and selected BESS developers
(“BESPA”) dated 16.07.2025 & 28.07.2025 were executed. APDISCOMs
filed a petition No OP 65 of 2025 before State Commission on 1.10.2025,
seeking approval of BESSA and BESPA, in which Impugned Order was
passed. It is of relevance to mention that under Article 1.1 of the BESSA,
Page 11 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
the trading margin of 7 paisa /Unit is agreed to be payable to NHPC by
APDISCOM for making the BESS capacity available, in additional to the
Applicable Tariff under BESPA. State Commission in the impugned Order
notes that it being the standalone BESS project procured purely on
capacity basis ( Rs/MW/Month), and thereafter deliberating about the role
and risk involved on the part of NHPC and applying the option available
in the BESS guidelines, rejects the trading margin of 7 paisa per unit and
instead approved trading margin of .5 % of capacity charges and directs
amendment of BESSA accordingly. Relevant paragraph is extracted
hereunder
“By choosing the 7 paise metric instead of the 0.5% capacity metric
offered in the same MoP guideline, NHPC is extracting an
administrative fee that is more than 7.5 times higher than the latter.
This is an unjustified burden on AP consumers for a purely
administrative, pass-through service. NHPC cites Regulation 8(1) of
the CERC Trading Licence Regulations to justify the 7 paise.
However, CERC trading margins are meant to compensate
traditional traders who assume the risk of volume fluctuations, open
access, and energy market volatility. In this back-to-back
BESSA/BESPA arrangement, NHPC assumes absolutely zero
energy-volume risk. They are a "BESS Implementing Agency" (BIA)
executing a fixed-capacity tolling agreement. Their compensation
should reflect fixed administrative effort (a percentage of the capacity
charge), not an energy trader's volume-based markup.
As regards the contention of NHPC that other State Commissions
permitted 7 paise per unit trading margin, it may be noted that
APERC is an independent statutory body whose primary mandate
under Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act, 2003, is to regulate
electricity purchase and procurement to protect the consumers of
Andhra Pradesh and it is not legally bound by the decisions State
Commissions.
Therefore, the Commission rejects the unjustified 7 paise/kWh
margin and directs the DISCOMs to cap the same at 0.5% of the
Capacity Charges, as explicitly provided as an option in Clause
2.G(4) of the MoP Guidelines. The DISCOMs shall amend the
BESSAs appropriately to reflect the same.”
Page 12 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
22. As a general principle, where a tariff has been discovered through
a transparent competitive bidding process and is placed before the
Appropriate Commission for adoption under Section 63 of the Electricity
Act, 2003, the nature and scope of the Commission's jurisdiction are
materially distinct from its tariff determination powers under Section 62.
Under Section 63, the Commission is not required to undertake an
independent determination of tariff; rather, its function is to satisfy itself
that the bidding process has been conducted in a transparent manner, in
accordance with the statutory framework and the guidelines issued by the
Central Government, and that the tariff has emerged from genuine
competitive bidding. Upon such satisfaction, the Commission is ordinarily
obliged to adopt the discovered tariff and cannot, under the guise of tariff
scrutiny, rewrite the commercial bargain negotiated by the contracting
parties. However, the position becomes slightly nuanced when dealing
with a trading margin. Trading margin is not merely a matter of contract; it
is also a regulated subject under the Electricity Act and the applicable
Trading Licence Regulations. Furthermore, Section 86(1)(b) of the
Electricity Act, 2003 empowers a State Commission to regulate the
electricity purchase and procurement process of distribution licensees,
including the price at which electricity is procured. The exercise of such
regulatory jurisdiction is ultimately anchored in the protection of consumer
interest and the maintenance of regulatory discipline within the electricity
sector.
23. Hon’ble Supreme Court in Energy Watchdog v. CERC, (2017) 14
SCC 80, and Jaipur Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. MB Power (Madhya
Pradesh) Ltd., (2024) 8 SCC 513, recognised that even in matters arising
under Section 63, the Commission is not reduced to a mere post office
Page 13 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
and remains entitled to undertake scrutiny within the confines of the
applicable statutory and regulatory framework, having due regard to
consumer interest and other relevant considerations. Likewise, in All
India Power Engineer Federation v. Sasan Power Ltd., (2017) 1 SCC
487, decided on 08.12.2016, the Hon’ble Supreme Court emphasised that
contractual arrangements affecting the tariff payable by consumers are
subject to regulatory scrutiny, having regard to the public interest
underlying electricity tariff determination. That contractual consent cannot,
by itself, dispense with compliance with the statutory and regulatory
framework governing electricity procurement.
24. In the present case, the controversy pertains to the trading margin
payable to the Appellant. It is an admitted position that the selection of the
Intermediary, namely the Appellant, was not undertaken through a
competitive bidding process. It is further undisputed that the trading
margin of 7 paise/kWh stipulated in the Battery Energy Storage Purchase
Agreement (BESSA) was agreed by the contracting parties having regard
to the provisions contained in the Guidelines for Procurement and
Utilisation of Battery Energy Storage Systems dated 10.03.2022 ("BESS
Guidelines, 2022").
25. Therefore, the issue requiring determination is not merely whether
the parties had mutually agreed upon a trading margin of Rs 0.07 per kWh.
The real question is whether such agreed trading margin is permissible
and consistent with the governing regulatory framework, particularly when
the procurement of the Intermediary was not through a competitive
process and the transaction is expressly governed by the BESS
Guidelines, 2022. In other words, the validity of the agreed trading margin
must be examined in the context of the applicable statutory and regulatory
provisions rather than solely on the basis of contractual consensus
Page 14 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
between the parties. In this regard, it is apposite to refer to the relevant
provisions of the BESS Guidelines dated 10.03.2022, which read as
under:
“4. The Intermediary Procurer shall enter into the Battery Storage
Purchase Agreement (BESPA) / Power Purchase Agreement with
the Developer(s) and enter into a Battery Storage Sale Agreement
(BESSA) /Power Sale Agreement with the distribution licensee(s)/
consumer(s). The BESSA shall contain the relevant provisions of the
BESPA on a back-to-back basis. The Intermediary Procurer shall be
entitled to charge trading margin of seven paise/kWh or 0.5% of the
Capacity Charges (as applicable) from the Buying entity / Procurer
for purchase and sale of such energy/capacity.”
26. A plain reading of the applicable Guidelines suggests that the
trading margin payable to an intermediary may be determined in either of
two ways, namely: (i) 7 paise per unit of electricity traded, or (ii) 0.5% of
the applicable capacity charges. The expression "as applicable" appears
to indicate that the applicable margin would depend upon the nature of
the transaction and the charging structure adopted. Prima facie, therefore,
the Guidelines contemplate two distinct charging mechanisms rather than
authorising a regulatory authority to freely replace one agreed mechanism
with another after the conclusion of the bidding process and execution of
the contract.
27. In the present case, as recorded in the Impugned Order and not
disputed by the Appellant, the Respondent DISCOMs themselves supply
power for charging the battery and subsequently draw back the stored
energy. Under Article V of the BESSA, the Respondents have agreed to
procure 500 MW/1000 MWh of "BESS Capacity" arranged by the
Appellant under back-to-back BESPAs executed with the Battery Energy
Page 15 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
Storage System Developers. Prima facie we are of the view that
transaction, has a significant capacity-based component, with the
developers being compensated primarily for making the storage capacity
available rather than for sale of energy generated by them.
28. Appellant has contended that the parties, with full knowledge of the
commercial structure of the project, expressly agreed upon a trading
margin of 7 paise/unit in the executed BESSA. It is further asserted that
the State Commission had already taken cognisance of the said provision
in its communication dated 04.07.2025 and no objection was raised at that
stage. According to the Appellant, once the tariff emerged through a
competitive bidding process and the trading margin formed an integral
component of the executed contractual framework, the Commission's role
was confined to examining conformity with the applicable Guidelines and
public interest, and did not extend to rewriting a negotiated commercial
term between the parties. The Appellant has argued that the substitution
of the agreed trading margin of 7 paise/unit with a margin linked to 0.5%
of capacity charges amounts not merely to regulatory scrutiny but to
modification of a concluded bargain.
29. We are of the considered view that the rival contentions advanced
by the parties, namely, whether the trading margin of 7 paise per unit,
having been expressly agreed upon by the Respondent, ought to govern
the transaction, or whether the State Commission was justified in
substituting the agreed trading margin by applying the alternative
stipulation of 0.5% of the Capacity Charges envisaged under the BESS
Guidelines, require detailed examination. Having regard to the facts and
circumstances of the present case, we are not inclined to render any
conclusive finding on the said issue at this interlocutory stage. The matter
Page 16 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
warrants comprehensive consideration on merits, which shall be
undertaken at the time of final hearing of the Appeal.
30. It is a settled principle of law that interlocutory mandatory directions,
particularly directing adopting an alternative course of action, are not to
be granted lightly or as a matter of course. Such relief, being exceptional
in nature and approximately the final relief at an interim stage, may be
granted only in circumstances where the Court is satisfied that the
Applicant/Appellant has established a strong prima facie case, that the
balance of convenience is demonstrably in favour of the applicant, and
that irreparable prejudice would ensue if such relief were withheld (
“Dorab Cawasji Warden v. Coomi Sorab Warden” ,; (1990) 2 SCC 117,
“Hammad Ahmed v. Abdul Majeed”, ;(2019) 14 SCC 1, “Samir Narain
Bhojwani v. Aurora Properties & Investments,; (2018) 17 SCC 203).
Therefore, the grant of mandatory directions at the interlocutory stage,
being in the nature of final relief, must be confined to cases where the
equities are clear, the obligation is undisputed, and the denial of
immediate enforcement would defeat the ends of justice.
31. In the present case, considering the averments made by parties,
and deliberations recorded hereinabove, we are of the considered view
that appellant has not been able to make out a prima facie case for
passing any interim direction for adoption of trading margin of 7 paisa /unit
instead of .5 % of capacity charge as provided in the Impugned Order.
Having regard to the settled principles governing interlocutory mandatory
relief, we find no justification for granting the interim relief sought at this
stage. The application, therefore, does not merit acceptance and
accordingly the prayer for interim relief is declined. It is, however, clarified
Page 17 of 18

Order in IA No. 862 of 2026 in Appeal No. 194 of 2026
